Use when asked to implement an API as an MCP server, wrap a REST API in MCP tools, add tool coverage for new endpoints to an existing MCP server, plan API-to-tool parity, or discover undocumented API usage behind a web interface.
- fossa-list: Show the FOSSA posture for exactly the two GTM-demo projects — license-conflict-demo and react2shell-app — with their issues and impact risk scores, and nothing else from the org. Use when asked to list, show, pull, or score "the demo projects", "the two projects", "license and react2shell", or to demo the FOSSA MCP integration without the rest of the portfolio on screen.
- fossa-protect: Turn a project's FOSSA findings into NeuVector runtime controls and push them to the cluster. Two tracks — vulnerability findings become WAF sensors (regex-matched request inspection); license-conflict findings become a workload quarantine (network isolation / deploy hold). Use when asked to mitigate, compensate for, or "protect against" CVEs found by FOSSA, to write WAF sensors/rules for a project's dependencies, to quarantine or "wall off" a workload with an unresolved license conflict, or whenever FOSSA findings and NeuVector need to be connected. Also use when asked which projects are available to protect or how critical each one is, and when asked to review or roll back sensors or quarantines created this way.
- fossa-suggest-score: Rank FOSSA projects by remediation urgency using a custom impact risk score that adds reachability and exposure to CVSS and EPSS. Use when asked which projects need remediation, how to prioritize FOSSA findings, to build or suggest a custom risk/impact score, to triage a FOSSA portfolio, or whenever FOSSA severity is being questioned as a prioritization signal.
- handoff: Write a handoff document that lets the current work continue in a fresh session, then clear. Use when a session has grown long or expensive, when the Stop hook nudges about session length, at a natural task boundary, or whenever the user asks for a handoff, to "wrap up this session", or to start fresh without losing context.
- lab-image-build: Build and push a container image for an ash4d lab repo using the in-cluster kaniko job, then verify the tag actually landed in Harbor. Use this skill whenever the user wants to build an image, cut a release, bump a version and ship it, push to registry.ash4d.com, rebuild a lab service's container, or asks why a build failed or whether a tag is really in the registry. Also use it when a rollout needs an image that does not exist yet.
- rick-preferences: Load Rick's working preferences before doing substantial work for him. Use this skill at the start of ANY non-trivial task, and specifically whenever the work involves — writing prose he will send or publish, any claim about his career or resume, infrastructure, containers, deployment, scripting, git or a repo, the ash4d lab or _portfolio or a darthzen repo, a deal or demo or customer conversation, a visual artifact or deck or infographic, credentials or keys, or destructive and irreversible actions on lab equipment. Also use it whenever he says his preferences were not followed, asks what his preferences say, or references the preferences folder. Read the routing table, then read only the file the task needs.
- sdf1-power: Control rack power for sdf1 through the DLI switch and test whether the lab recovers from a power loss. Use this skill whenever the user wants to cut, restore, or cycle power to sdf1, the disk array or the monitor; whenever they ask whether the lab will come back after an outage, whether the BIOS is set to power on after AC loss, or whether Wake-on-LAN works; whenever they want to power sdf1 on or off remotely, reboot it at the hardware level, or run a DR or power-failure test; and whenever they ask how much power the lab is drawing. If the user wants to pause individual lab services to reclaim CPU rather than cut power at the wall, use sdf1-toggle instead.
- sdf1-toggle: Turn ash4d lab services on sdf1 on and off to reclaim CPU, memory and disk IO — pausing Fleet bundles and scaling workloads to zero, then restoring them. Use this skill whenever the user names a lab service and wants it shut down, paused, stopped, suspended, disabled, spun down, turned off, re-enabled, resumed or brought back (openchoreo, buzz, ai/ollama, emby/media, neuvector/security, the agent workers); whenever they say "toggle" anything on sdf1; whenever they ask what's currently running or what's eating CPU and want to act on it; and whenever they mention freeing up resources or quieting the lab before heavy GPU or training work. If the user invokes this without naming a service, ask which one rather than guessing.
- supacode-cli: Control Supacode from the terminal. Use when running Supacode CLI commands, managing worktrees, tabs, and surfaces programmatically, or when inside a Supacode terminal session.
- supacode-deeplinks: Control Supacode with supacode:// URLs. Always prefer the supacode CLI when it is available; use deeplinks only from scripts, other apps, or terminals where the supacode CLI is not installed.

Use this skill whenever the user mentions preparing for a 1:1, one-on-one, weekly with an SE, coaching conversation, or check-in with a direct report; whenever they paste notes from a 1:1 and want them processed; and whenever they ask "what should I cover with [name] this week?" — even if they never say "agenda."

Use this skill whenever the user asks for an infographic, one-pager, visual summary, leave-behind, poster, or "something visual I can send"; and whenever another skill (like present-impress) needs an infographic-quality composition. - dataviz: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.

content.text:
The edit path already exists — it's in the Inspector, in a "Grid" section that appears when you select a module.

How it works:

- **Select a module on the canvas**, and the Inspector (right panel) shows a **Grid** section: an 8×5 replica of the module's device page, with every module on that page shown in its live slot (this module at full color, neighbors dimmed).
- **Click any button in that mini-grid** — the module moves there and gets **pinned** (a pin icon appears). The rest of the page reflows around it automatically.
- **Unpin** (the link button next to the pin icon) hands the slot back to automatic flow placement.

The underlying model, for context:

- Auto-assignment is `reflowGrid()` in `Sources/ZoiaCanvas/Model/PatchDocument.swift:404` — unpinned modules get packed first-fit in signal-flow order after every structural change. Pinned modules never move during reflow, so a manual placement sticks.
- The click-to-pin UI is `gridSection` / `gridButtons` in `Sources/ZoiaCanvas/Views/InspectorView.swift:69-131`.
- If pinning pushes a page over 40 buttons, the section shows a red "Page over 40 buttons — export is blocked" warning and export refuses with a per-page reason.

One caveat flagged in the code itself: button span is assumed to be one button per active block, marked as unverified against real hardware — worth checking against the pedal on a multi-block module before trusting a tight layout.

The minimap on the canvas is display-only; all editing goes through the Inspector's grid. If you'd rather drag modules directly on the minimap, that would be new work — say the word and I'll add it.

**Pinning is gone — placement is now sticky:**
- A module gets a slot once (on add, drop, or import) and keeps it. Cables, deletions, and edits elsewhere never move it.

- Imported layouts stay verbatim, including authored overlaps.

Every drag step re-derives displacement from a pre-drag snapshot, so a neighbor pushed aside returns the moment you drag elsewhere; release keeps what the preview shows. Grabbing one of a multi-button module's own buttons drags by that button.

Opening a .bin swaps in a fresh document, so ⌫/⌘⌫ were deleting from the dead one: the selection binding (still live) cleared, closing the inspector, while the canvas rendered the new document where the module survived. The monitors now reinstall whenever the document identity changes. Plain ⌫ was equally broken after a file open; right-click worked because the context menu rebuilds each render.

A 30-second check on your side: open a .bin, select a module, ⌘⌫ — and drag something around the inspector grid. Both issues are fixed and the launch behavior is in. Full suite passes (223 tests). Still nothing committed.

**The crash.** My Cmd+Del fix exposed a latent bug rather than introducing one: the inspector's binding closures (name field, color/page/option pickers, param sliders) captured an array *index* into `document.modules`. Deleting the selected module while its inspector is open lets AppKit query one of those bindings before SwiftUI tears the panel down — subscript past the end, fatal error. Before the monitor fix, shortcut delete never actually mutated the live document after a file open, so the window never opened. Every escaping binding now re-resolves the module by id at access time (`liveIndex`) and returns a harmless default if it's gone. Deletes that go through id-based document methods (`setOption`, `setParam`, `moveModule`) were already guarded.

**Launch restore.** The app now reopens the last successfully opened patch at startup instead of untitled. It stores a bookmark (not a path, so it survives the file being moved) on every successful open — importer, Finder drop, and double-click all funnel through the same function. If the file no longer exists, the bookmark is cleared quietly and you get untitled; a corrupt file still surfaces the normal error alert.

One flag: both fixes are verified by reading, build, and the model-level tests — the crash itself was UI-timing and I can't drive the GUI from here, so the real confirmation is you pressing ⌘⌫ on a selected module again. If it still throws, I'd want the first few frames of the stack trace, which will name the exact view.

Fixed, and this time reproduced rather than inferred. Full suite passes (224 tests, including the new regression test).

What happened:

- I built a test that hosts the real `InspectorView` in a window, deletes the module underneath it, and pumps the run loop. It died with your exact fatal error — no keyboard involved.
- The surviving culprit was the param value label (`InspectorView.swift:233`): a `ForEach` row closure that still read `document.modules[index]` with the captured index. My previous pass fixed the control *bindings* but assumed row content only re-evaluates after the outer body re-checks the module. The reproduction proved that wrong — SwiftUI re-runs the row closure on its own after the deletion.
- The slider and label now share one guarded read (`paramFraction`) that re-resolves the module by id and returns 0 if it's gone. With that change the reproducer passes.

The regression test (`InspectorTeardownTests`) stays in the suite, so any future captured-index read in the inspector will fail the build instead of crashing the app. The launch-restore and sticky-drag work from earlier is unchanged. 4	/// Per-port signal history feeding the cable and module animations,
5	/// modeled on Bespoke Synth's trio of NoteHistory (gate events sweep
6	/// down the cable over 250 ms), IModulator's smoothed-value recent
7	/// change (the blue↔red modulation overlay), and the RollingBuffer viz
8	/// tap (the cable drawn as the waveform it carries).
9	///
10	/// Written by PatchRuntime at the end of every render block and read by
11	/// the UI through AudioEngine's snapshot methods; the RuntimeBox lock
12	/// serializes the two sides, so nothing here locks.
13	final class SignalTap {
14	    /// Bespoke NOTE_HISTORY_LENGTH: seconds for an event to travel the
15	    /// full cable, and the note-highlight decay time on modules.
16	    static let historyLength = 0.25
17	    /// Bespoke NoteHistory::kHistorySize.
18	    static let historySize = 100
19	    /// Rolling audio window shown along a cable, ~21 ms at 48 kHz.
20	    static let vizSize = 1024
21	    /// Gate-high threshold, matching the runtime's module semantics.
22	    static let gateThreshold: Float = 0.5
23	
24	    struct GateEvent {
25	        var on = false
26	        var time = 0.0
27	    }
28	
29	    // MARK: Gate history (CV ports)
30	
31	    private var history = [GateEvent](repeating: GateEvent(), count: SignalTap.historySize)
32	    private var historyPos = 0
33	    private(set) var lastOnEventTime = -999.0
34	    private var gateHigh = false
35	
36	    // MARK: Recent change (CV ports)
37	
38	    private(set) var lastValue: Float = 0
39	    private(set) var smoothedValue: Float = 0
40	    var recentChange: Float { lastValue - smoothedValue }
41	
42	    // MARK: Audio viz ring (audio ports)
43	
44	    private(set) var isAudio = false
45	    private var viz = [Float](repeating: 0, count: SignalTap.vizSize)
46	    private var vizHead = 0
47	
48	    func updateCV(_ value: Float, time: Double, blocksPerSecond: Double) {
49	        let high = value >= Self.gateThreshold
50	        if high != gateHigh {
51	            gateHigh = high
52	            if high { lastOnEventTime = time }
53	            historyPos = (historyPos + 1) % Self.historySize
54	            history[historyPos] = GateEvent(on: high, time: time)
55	        }
56	        // Bespoke IModulator::Poll — exp2 blend is framerate-independent,
57	        // so updating per control block instead of per UI frame keeps the
58	        // same time constant.
59	        let blend = Float(exp2(-9.65784 / max(blocksPerSecond, 1)))
60	        lastValue = value
61	        smoothedValue = smoothedValue * blend + value * (1 - blend)
62	    }
63	
64	    func updateAudio(_ samples: [Float]) {
65	        isAudio = true
66	        for s in samples {
67	            viz[vizHead] = s
68	            vizHead = (vizHead + 1) % Self.vizSize
69	        }
70	    }
71	
72	    /// Events newest-first, ending with the first one older than the
73	    /// travel window — the Bespoke draw loop needs that one terminator.
74	    func recentEvents(now: Double) -> [GateEvent] {
75	        var events: [GateEvent] = []
76	        for ago in 0..<Self.historySize {
77	            let event = history[(historyPos + Self.historySize - ago) % Self.historySize]
78	            guard event.time > 0 else { break }
79	            events.append(event)
80	            if now - event.time >= Self.historyLength { break }
81	        }
82	        return events
83	    }

85	    /// Samples newest-first: index i is the sample i frames ago, the
86	    /// order Bespoke's cable draw consumes (newest at the source end).
87	    func vizSnapshot() -> [Float] {
88	        var snapshot = [Float](repeating: 0, count: Self.vizSize)
89	        for ago in 0..<Self.vizSize {
90	            snapshot[ago] = viz[(vizHead + Self.vizSize - 1 - ago) % Self.vizSize]
91	        }

93	    }

95	    /// Bespoke IDrawableModule::DrawFrame audio highlight: fourth root
96	    /// of mean square over the last ≤500 samples, ×3, clamped, ×0.15.
97	    func audioHighlight() -> Float {
98	        let count = min(500, Self.vizSize)
99	        var meanSquare: Float = 0
100	        for ago in 0..<count {
101	            let s = viz[(vizHead + Self.vizSize - 1 - ago) % Self.vizSize]
102	            meanSquare += s * s
103	        }
104	        meanSquare /= Float(count)
105	        let mag = min(max(meanSquare.squareRoot().squareRoot() * 3, 0), 1)

107	    }

111	    func noteHighlight(now: Double) -> Float {

117	/// The Bespoke cable animation formulas, kept pure for tests.
118	enum CableAnimation {
119	    /// Seconds per bar for the tempo throb on a traveling pulse.
120	    /// Bespoke syncs to its transport; ZoiaCanvas has none, so this is
121	    /// fixed at Bespoke's default 120 BPM 4/4 bar.
122	    static let barSeconds = 2.0
123	
124	    /// Line width of a lit gate segment (PatchCable.cpp:260): starts 5×,
125	    /// decays to 2×, with a bar-synced cosine shimmer on top.
126	    static func litWidth(elapsed: Double, sinceEvent: Double) -> Double {
127	        2 + min(max(1 - elapsed * 0.7, 0), 1) * 3
128	            + cos(sinceEvent * .pi * 8 / barSeconds) * 0.3
129	    }
130	
131	    /// Audio sample → cable displacement fraction: signed square root
132	    /// soft-compression, clamped ±1 (PatchCable.cpp:359).
133	    static func compress(_ sample: Float) -> Float {
134	        let c = sample.magnitude.squareRoot() * (sample < 0 ? -1 : 1)
135	        return min(max(c, -1), 1)
136	    }
137	
138	    /// Modulation overlay alpha for a normalized recent-change delta
139	    /// (PatchCable.cpp:216): flares on change, fades at rest.
140	    static func modulationAlpha(_ delta: Float) -> Float {
141	        abs(1 - (1 - delta) * (1 - delta)) * (150.0 / 255.0)
142	    }
143	
144	    /// Bespoke kHighlightGrowAmount: world points a module frame
145	    /// inflates per unit of highlight.
146	    static let highlightGrow: CGFloat = 40
147	}
148	
149	/// Arc-length parameterization of a cable path, so pulses travel at
150	/// constant speed and waveform samples space evenly on beziers and
151	/// angular routes alike.
152	struct PathSampler {
153	    private var points: [CGPoint]
154	    private var cumulative: [CGFloat]
155	    private(set) var length: CGFloat
156	
157	    init(polyline: [CGPoint]) {
158	        points = polyline.count > 1 ? polyline : polyline + polyline
159	        var cumulative: [CGFloat] = [0]
160	        var total: CGFloat = 0
161	        for i in 1..<points.count {
162	            total += hypot(points[i].x - points[i - 1].x, points[i].y - points[i - 1].y)
163	            cumulative.append(total)
164	        }
165	        self.cumulative = cumulative
166	        length = total
167	    }
168	
169	    init(from: CGPoint, control1: CGPoint, control2: CGPoint, to: CGPoint,
170	         segments: Int = 48) {
171	        var sampled: [CGPoint] = []
172	        for i in 0...segments {
173	            let t = CGFloat(i) / CGFloat(segments)
174	            let u = 1 - t
175	            sampled.append(CGPoint(
176	                x: u * u * u * from.x + 3 * u * u * t * control1.x
177	                    + 3 * u * t * t * control2.x + t * t * t * to.x,
178	                y: u * u * u * from.y + 3 * u * u * t * control1.y
179	                    + 3 * u * t * t * control2.y + t * t * t * to.y))
180	        }
181	        self.init(polyline: sampled)
182	    }
183	
184	    /// Point at an arc-length fraction 0…1.
185	    func point(at fraction: CGFloat) -> CGPoint {
186	        let target = min(max(fraction, 0), 1) * length
187	        guard length > 0 else { return points[0] }
188	        var low = 0
189	        var high = cumulative.count - 1
190	        while low + 1 < high {
191	            let mid = (low + high) / 2
192	            if cumulative[mid] <= target { low = mid } else { high = mid }
193	        }
194	        let span = cumulative[high] - cumulative[low]
195	        let t = span > 0 ? (target - cumulative[low]) / span : 0
196	        return CGPoint(
197	            x: points[low].x + (points[high].x - points[low].x) * t,
198	            y: points[low].y + (points[high].y - points[low].y) * t)
199	    }
200	
201	    /// Unit normal at an arc-length fraction, for waveform displacement.
202	    func perpendicular(at fraction: CGFloat) -> CGPoint {
203	        let target = min(max(fraction, 0), 1) * length
204	        guard length > 0 else { return CGPoint(x: 0, y: -1) }
205	        var low = 0
206	        var high = cumulative.count - 1
207	        while low + 1 < high {
208	            let mid = (low + high) / 2
209	            if cumulative[mid] <= target { low = mid } else { high = mid }
210	        }
211	        let dx = points[high].x - points[low].x
212	        let dy = points[high].y - points[low].y
213	        let len = hypot(dx, dy)
214	        guard len > 0 else { return CGPoint(x: 0, y: -1) }
215	        return CGPoint(x: -dy / len, y: dx / len)
216	    }
217	}

All three pieces are done — 228 tests pass, and every module in the demo patch is confirmed implemented in the audio runtime. Nothing committed.

**AnimationDemo.bin** (sent above, also at the project root — the app will reopen it on launch once you've opened it once). Eight modules on one page:
- CLOCK (square LFO ~1.1 Hz) → sequencer clock and VCA level: **gate pulses** on both cables, **clock flash** on the modules, live-cable dimming.
- SWEEP (sine LFO ~0.3 Hz) → filter cutoff and pan position: the **red/blue modulation overlay**, slow and continuous — the best surface for judging it.
- SEQ steps → oscillator pitch (~220–560 Hz): modulation overlay in bursts.
- OSC → FILTER → VCA → PAN → OUT: **waveform wires** and the **audio module glow**, with the VCA chop making the glow pulse.

**Cable pickup.** Dragging from an input port that has a cable now unplugs its newest cable and puts the freed end on your cursor — the source end stays anchored. Drop on another input to move it (your VCA→speakers-to-panner case), drop on empty space to disconnect. Strength travels with the plug, and dropping back on the same port is a clean cancel. Dragging an input with no cable still moves the module.

**Save.** ⌘S, a File → Save Patch menu item, and a toolbar Save button (Open's icon changed to a folder to free the standard save glyph). Saves write back to the opened file; an untitled patch asks for a home once, then saves silently. The window title shows `name *` while there are unsaved changes, and the Save button disables when clean. Tracking covers everything that reaches the .bin — structure, params, grid slots, pages, names, colors — and deliberately ignores canvas drags, which never export. Export (⌘E) still writes a copy without adopting it.

Verified by tests and build; the two things only you can judge remain the pickup gesture's feel and the demo patch's sound (the LFO rate and pitch curves in the runtime are marked as unmeasured assumptions, so tempo may differ from my estimates — the animations show regardless).
